Rejoice in that day, and leap for joy, for behold, your reward is great in heaven, for their fathers did the same thing to the prophets.
b: This passage records the "blessings" Jesus declared to his disciples on the level place. Jesus tells them that those who are poor, hungry, weeping, and persecuted in this age are in fact blessed, because they will receive blessing and comfort in God's kingdom. These words overturn the world's values: Jesus turns worldly poverty and suffering into spiritual blessing, stressing that in God's kingdom true happiness comes from trusting and being faithful to God.

Jesus especially mentions those who are persecuted for his sake, who will have a great reward in heaven. This passage stresses that as followers of Christ we may face rejection and persecution from the world because of our faith, yet we should rejoice in it, because it shows we have a share in God's kingdom and that our reward is rich.

This passage teaches us that Jesus' gospel is not only about life in this age but also about eternal hope. When we face difficulties and challenges in life, we should remember the blessings Jesus spoke of, hold firm in faith, and not be swayed by worldly standards. True blessing lies in God's kingdom; we should fix our eyes on the eternal reward and believe God's promises.
q: When you face poverty, hunger, or weeping, how can you remember Jesus' promise and meet these challenges with faith?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for giving us Jesus Christ, who taught us what true blessing is. Help us to keep our faith in trials and difficulties, remembering that our reward in heaven is great. May we hold firm to our faith, live out the likeness of Christ, and draw strength from eternal hope. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: “But woe to you who are rich! For you have received your consolation.
Woe to you, you who are full now, for you will be hungry. Woe to you who laugh now, for you will mourn and weep.
Woe, when men speak well of you, for their fathers did the same thing to the false prophets.
b: This passage follows right after the "blessings" Jesus declared. Here Jesus points out that those who are rich, full, laughing, and spoken well of by the world in this age are in fact in woe. His words again overturn the values of society at that time: he shows that prosperity and satisfaction in this age are not the same as spiritual blessing, and may even become the root of future trouble.

Jesus especially stresses that those who chase after the pleasures and honors of this age may lose true happiness at God's judgment. This passage reminds us that worldly wealth and success often cause people to forget God, becoming self-satisfied and proud, and such an attitude leads to spiritual poverty and final loss.

This passage teaches us to be on guard against worldly temptation and not to let the prosperity and praise of this age lead us away from God's path. We should pursue spiritual riches, keep a humble and thankful heart, and set our eyes on God's kingdom and eternal blessing. We need to examine ourselves often, to make sure our hearts are not captivated by worldly glory but focused on seeking God's will.
q: When you enjoy the wealth and success of this age, how can you make sure they do not draw you away from God's will? How can you stay humble and thankful in those circumstances?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for reminding us through Jesus Christ not to be deceived by the wealth and honor of this age. Help us to keep a humble heart, to pursue spiritual abundance, and to hold reverence and gratitude before you. May our lives show the values of your kingdom and become a witness to your grace. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: “But I tell you who hear: love your enemies, do good to those who hate you,
bless those who curse you, and pray for those who mistreat you.
To him who strikes you on the cheek, offer also the other; and from him who takes away your cloak, don’t withhold your coat also.
Give to everyone who asks you, and don’t ask him who takes away your goods to give them back again.
“As you would like people to do to you, do exactly so to them.
b: This passage is Jesus' teaching to his disciples, stressing the highest expression of love and forgiveness. Jesus asks his followers to go beyond ordinary standards of behavior, and to treat even their enemies with love and kindness. This teaching challenges our natural reactions of justice and revenge, and calls us to replace resentment and retaliation with love and forgiveness.

Jesus' teachings such as "love your enemies" and "bless those who curse you" show the supernatural nature of the Christian life. We are called to love others with Jesus' love, not only those who love us but also those who hurt us. This demand of love is very high, but it is what Jesus expects, because he himself paid the price for our sins on the cross and showed this unconditional love.

This passage teaches us that the Christian life should be a life full of love and forgiveness. Our love should not be limited by outward circumstances or by what others do, but should be like Jesus' love, going beyond human limits to love everyone. Such love rests on our relationship with God, and it can change the world around us and let God's love flow out through us.
q: When you face enemies or unfair treatment, how are you willing to rely on God's strength to love them and respond in Jesus' way?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for teaching us through Jesus Christ the true meaning of love and forgiveness. Help us, when we face enemies and injustice, to respond with your love and kindness. May our lives show your love and become light and salt to this world. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: If you love those who love you, what credit is that to you? For even sinners love those who love them.
If you do good to those who do good to you, what credit is that to you? For even sinners do the same.
If you lend to those from whom you hope to receive, what credit is that to you? Even sinners lend to sinners, to receive back as much.
But love your enemies, and do good, and lend, expecting nothing back; and your reward will be great, and you will be children of the Most High; for he is kind toward the unthankful and evil.
“Therefore be merciful, even as your Father is also merciful.
b: This passage continues Jesus' teaching to his disciples and further stresses the surpassing nature of love and forgiveness. Jesus reminds us that if we only love those who love us, that is not enough to show Christ's love, because even sinners can do that. True love is loving those who do not love us, even our enemies, and only then can we reflect God's kindness.

Jesus' teaching challenges our way of thinking. He calls us to be good to those who do not deserve it, and to lend without expecting repayment. Such conduct shows our trust in God and our hope in his promise. Jesus promises that when we do this our reward will be great, and we will be called children of the Most High, because God is kind in just this way to those who do not deserve his grace.

This passage teaches us to follow God's mercy, and to show in our lives a love and kindness that go beyond ordinary standards. When we love others according to Jesus' teaching, we can become vessels of God's love and see God's kingdom come true in our lives. Such love changes not only ourselves but also the world we touch.
q: In your life, do you have opportunities to love, in a way that goes beyond the world's ways, those who do not deserve love? How can you show God's mercy?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for teaching us through Jesus Christ the true meaning of love. Help us in daily life to treat others with your mercy, going beyond worldly standards. May our lives reflect your kindness and become a witness to your love. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: Don’t judge, and you won’t be judged. Don’t condemn, and you won’t be condemned. Set free, and you will be set free.
“Give, and it will be given to you: good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over, will be given to you. For with the same measure you measure it will be measured back to you.”
b: This passage is Jesus' teaching to his disciples, stressing the importance of not judging, not condemning, and forgiving. Jesus points out that when we do not judge or condemn others, we ourselves will be spared judgment and condemnation. At the same time, Jesus calls us to a generous heart, willing to give to others, and promises that God will repay us with even greater grace.

Jesus says, "With the same measure you measure, it will be measured back to you," showing that the way we treat others directly affects how God treats us. This passage calls us to treat others with tolerance, kindness, and generosity, and then we will also receive rich returns from God.

This passage teaches us to be careful in what we say and do, not to judge or condemn others lightly, but to treat them with a tolerant and forgiving heart. We are also called to give to others generously, because God will repay us with the same generosity. When we follow these teachings, our lives will be full of God's blessing and grace.
q: When you face other people's mistakes or faults, can you treat them with tolerance and forgiveness? How can you put Jesus' teaching into practice in your life?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for teaching us through Jesus Christ the importance of not judging, not condemning, and forgiving. Help us in daily life to treat others with tolerance and generosity, and to respond to everyone with love. May our lives reflect your love and grace and become a blessing to others. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: He spoke a parable to them. “Can the blind guide the blind? Won’t they both fall into a pit?
A disciple is not above his teacher, but everyone when he is fully trained will be like his teacher.
b: In this passage Jesus uses a simple but profound picture to remind us to choose our teachers and examples carefully. He points out that if a blind man leads a blind man, both will fall into a pit. The picture teaches us to choose those with spiritual sight and wisdom to guide us, or we will face spiritual danger and loss.

Jesus also points out that a disciple is not above his teacher, which stresses the importance of learning. As disciples of Christ, we need to keep learning and following his teaching until our lives can reflect his likeness. Jesus is our supreme teacher, and our goal is, when fully trained, to be like him and live out a spiritually abundant life.

This passage teaches us that in following Christ we need to learn humbly, and to choose as our teachers those who can lead us into truth and spiritual growth. We should often examine our spiritual lives to make sure we are not deceived by spiritual blindness, but are following closely that supreme teacher, Jesus Christ.
q: In your spiritual life, whom have you chosen as teachers and examples? How have these choices affected your spiritual growth?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for teaching us through Jesus Christ how important it is to choose the right spiritual teachers and examples. Help us to keep learning on the road of following Christ and to become true disciples of Jesus. May our lives reflect his likeness and lead others onto the path of truth. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: Why do you see the speck of chaff that is in your brother’s eye, but don’t consider the beam that is in your own eye?

Or how can you tell your brother, ‘Brother, let me remove the speck of chaff that is in your eye,’ when you yourself don’t see the beam that is in your own eye? You hypocrite! First remove the beam from your own eye, and then you can see clearly to remove the speck of chaff that is in your brother’s eye.
b: This passage is Jesus' teaching to his disciples. He uses a vivid picture to expose a weakness of human nature: we easily see other people's faults while overlooking our own much greater ones. Jesus points out that before we criticize others, we should first reflect on ourselves and remove the "plank" from our own lives, and then we can see clearly to help others.

This teaching reminds us to be careful, and not to criticize or judge others lightly. Each of us has our own shortcomings, and we need to deal with our own problems first before we can truly help others. This attitude of self-examination and humility is an indispensable quality in the Christian life.

This passage teaches us that in life we should pay more attention to our own spiritual condition than to hurrying to point out others' mistakes. When we are willing to deal with our own problems first, our vision becomes clearer and we are better able to help others. We need to examine our hearts often and face other people's weaknesses with humility.
q: In your life, are you used to seeing others' mistakes first while overlooking your own shortcomings? How can you grow through self-examination and humility, and help others better?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for teaching us through Jesus Christ the importance of humility and self-examination. Help us, before criticizing others, to examine our own hearts first and remove the planks from our own lives. May our lives reflect Christ's love and humility, and may we help others with this attitude. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: For there is no good tree that produces rotten fruit; nor again a rotten tree that produces good fruit.
For each tree is known by its own fruit. For people don’t gather figs from thorns, nor do they gather grapes from a bramble bush.

The good man out of the good treasure of his heart brings out that which is good, and the evil man out of the evil treasure of his heart brings out that which is evil, for out of the abundance of the heart, his mouth speaks.
b: In this passage Jesus uses the picture of a tree and its fruit to teach us the importance of the condition of the heart. He points out that the quality of a tree determines the fruit it bears; in the same way, the condition of a person's heart determines his words and actions. Jesus stresses that a good person brings forth good from the good in his heart, while an evil person brings forth evil from the evil in his heart.

This picture reminds us to put weight on building up our inner life, and not only on outward behavior. True good deeds and upright words must come from a heart full of goodwill and love. Jesus teaches us that what fills the heart shows in our words and actions, so we need to examine our hearts often and make sure they are full of Christ's love and truth.

This passage teaches us that, as Christians, we should work to fill our hearts with goodness, love, and truth, so that our lives can bear good fruit. When our hearts are filled with God's love, our words and actions will naturally show that love and become a blessing to others. Let us keep pursuing growth in our inner life, and glorify God through it.
q: In your life, do you give weight to building up your heart and letting Christ's love and truth fill it? How can you bear good spiritual fruit in daily life?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for teaching us through Jesus Christ the importance of the inner life. Help us to examine our hearts often and let them be filled with your love and truth. May our words and actions bear good fruit, become a blessing to others, and glorify your name. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: “Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and don’t do the things which I say?
Everyone who comes to me, and hears my words, and does them, I will show you who he is like.

He is like a man building a house, who dug and went deep, and laid a foundation on the rock. When a flood arose, the stream broke against that house, and could not shake it, because it was founded on the rock.
But he who hears, and doesn’t do, is like a man who built a house on the earth without a foundation, against which the stream broke, and immediately it fell, and the ruin of that house was great.”
b: In this passage Jesus raises a question that is extremely important for the life of faith: why call him "Lord" and not do what he says? This is a deep reflection, reminding us that faith is not only verbal agreement or formal worship but needs to be lived out in daily life. Jesus stresses that true faith should be built on his words and shown through concrete action.

Jesus uses the picture of building a house to explain this. Those who hear his words and do them are like someone who builds a house on solid rock. Such a house stands firm in the storm and does not fall. This picture tells us that when we sink the foundation of our faith deep into Jesus' teaching, our lives can stand the test whatever trials or challenges come.

On the other hand, those who hear but do not do are like someone who builds a house on sand. Such a house may look much like the other from the outside, but it lacks a firm foundation and will surely fall when the storm comes. This reminds us that if our faith is only surface work, and Jesus' words are not truly woven into our lives, then when trouble comes our lives will not be able to bear it.
q: Are you putting Jesus' words into action in your life? How can you make sure the foundation of your faith is firm, so that you can stand in every kind of challenge?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for teaching us through Jesus Christ to build our faith on a solid foundation. Help us not only to hear the word but to do it, and let your word be rooted deeply in our lives. May our faith stand firm in the storm and bear witness to your great power. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: After he had finished speaking in the hearing of the people, he entered into Capernaum.
A certain centurion’s servant, who was dear to him, was sick and at the point of death.
When he heard about Jesus, he sent to him elders of the Jews, asking him to come and save his servant.
When they came to Jesus, they begged him earnestly, saying, “He is worthy for you to do this for him,
for he loves our nation, and he built our synagogue for us.”
Jesus went with them. When he was now not far from the house, the centurion sent friends to him, saying to him, “Lord, don’t trouble yourself, for I am not worthy for you to come under my roof.
Therefore I didn’t even think myself worthy to come to you; but say the word, and my servant will be healed.
For I also am a man placed under authority, having under myself soldiers. I tell this one, ‘Go!’ and he goes; and to another, ‘Come!’ and he comes; and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.”
When Jesus heard these things, he marveled at him, and turned and said to the multitude who followed him, “I tell you, I have not found such great faith, no, not in Israel.”
Those who were sent, returning to the house, found that the servant who had been sick was well.
b: This passage records the story of Jesus healing a centurion's servant. The centurion's faith is highly praised in the Gospels. He was a Gentile, yet he had deep trust in and reverence for Jesus; he even felt unworthy to meet Jesus and only asked that Jesus say a word and his servant would be healed. Such faith and humility made Jesus marvel at him, and Jesus used it to teach the people.

The centurion's faith was not merely an abstract belief but was based on his understanding of authority. He understood that as a man under authority he could give orders, and in the same way he believed that Jesus had supernatural authority and could heal his servant with just a word. This trust in Jesus' authority became the model of faith in the Gospels.

Jesus' praise of the centurion tells us that true faith does not come from our status or background, but from our complete trust in and submission to Jesus. This reminds us that in our own lives we should also learn the centurion's faith and humility, believing in Jesus' power and that every word of his carries power to change our circumstances.
q: When you face difficulties, do you, like the centurion, trust wholeheartedly in Jesus' authority? How can you depend more deeply on his word in your life of faith?
Truth Transmission, Lesson 135: The Power of Thinking

"Thinking" is a very important process. It makes our ideas possible. Many studies and plans begin with a single thought and, through repeated thinking and trying, gradually move toward success! A thought is like a seed: though small, it can grow into a great tree. The great discoveries and inventions in human history were inspiration and thoughts that God gave to people; when people believe, think them over repeatedly until they become a conviction, and then act on them, they can accomplish God's heart and work.

God longs for us to take part in his plan. God puts his heart into our hearts, and he wants us to take part in his work through our "asking" and "thinking." "Accomplishing" is God's work; our responsibility is to "ask" and to "think."

When we "ask" and "think," God can accomplish. It is like a woman praying for a child. When she conceives, she has already "received"; she no longer needs to pray, yet it is not yet "accomplished"! She must go through the process of carrying the child until the time of birth comes and the child is born, and that is "accomplished"! It was like Hannah, who had no child and kept pouring out her heart in prayer at the temple. God spoke through the priest Eli, saying, "May the God of Israel grant your petition that you have asked of him." Hannah believed the priest's word and received it; she got up and ate and was no longer sad, because in her heart she had already received God's promise. She went home and lay with her husband, and God let her conceive, until the child was born and grew up, and she came to the temple to fulfill her vow. It was because she had already received and taken hold of the promise, and the promise was fulfilled, that she gave glory to God and offered a sacrifice to him.

When we have a need, a prayer arises. When God speaks, he answers our prayer, and when God grants what we ask, we have received the promise. We no longer need to keep asking; we should begin to think, to think in our hearts, to carry the promised word of God like a child in the womb. So we need to begin to practice the process of "thinking" that lies between "asking" and "accomplishing."

We should begin, by faith and by the Holy Spirit, to picture God's promise as the blueprint in our hearts, becoming the substance and evidence of faith. This can bring out the action of faith, applying it until it is accomplished, and then the promise is fulfilled. So the promise is received, the application is done, and the fulfillment is taken hold of. We need to practice this process, but the prerequisite is that we first seek until God speaks and promises to us, and only then do we think through that promise. It is not thinking out of thin air, nor asking wrongly according to our own desires, but thinking with substance and evidence.

From "receiving" to "accomplishing" takes a period of time. If we doubt or give up, it is like a "miscarriage" or an "abortion," and God's promise cannot be accomplished. The fulfillment of God's promise needs time, a process, faith, carrying, nurturing, and above all patience. So we must be patient in heart and wait calmly. Those who wait for the Lord will surely be blessed.

"Thinking" is a very powerful tool. Right "thinking" can let us experience what God does. We must be careful about what we "think," and not give Satan an opening. We should use our "thinking" well and dare to dream boldly for the Lord!

The laws of the spiritual realm and the laws of the natural world that God created have something in common: they are the channel of exchange between the spiritual realm and the natural world. This is the law by which God works in the natural world through the spiritual realm, so we need to understand:
God's Promised Word

God first speaks and promises us, because there is not one word of God that does not carry power. When God speaks, we begin to think, to think about God's word, and then faith arises. When we think it through and understand, God's word produces living faith within me, a lively faith, and this lively faith begins to produce a dream in our hearts. This dream is a kind of seeing in the heart; it sees the blueprint of what God will accomplish in his promise, and it becomes the substance and evidence of our faith. After that we begin to use words of faith to speak out God's word, and when we speak God's word by faith, God's word releases power and brings out authority, accomplishing in the natural world what God wants to accomplish, and so God's work is fulfilled. So these four principles are very important: the principle of thinking, the principle of faith, the principle of dreaming, and the principle of speaking. Through thinking, faith, dreaming, and speaking we can communicate with God: thinking becomes our thought, faith becomes our substance, dreaming becomes our vision, and speaking becomes our declaration. When we act this way by faith, God's promised word is fulfilled.

The devil imitates and disguises himself with deceptive words. His thinking is thoughts of worry and fear; the faith he gives us is negative, pessimistic faith; the nightmares he brings are dark, gray pictures; and the words he brings are words of complaint and cursing.

God also trained Abraham's faith through these principles. Abraham is called the father of faith, and his faith was nurtured slowly, from small to great. In training his faith, God first changed his name, calling him Abraham, which means father of many nations, and changed his wife Sarai to Sarah, which means mother of many nations. They called each other by name every day, which was declaring themselves father and mother of many nations. By hearing, they thought about what it would be like to become the father and mother of many nations, and they began to think about God's promise.
God took him to look at the stars in the sky and the sand on the seashore.

He promised him, "So shall your offspring be," as many as the stars of the sky and the sand on the seashore. So every time Abraham saw the stars in the sky or the sand by the sea, he looked and thought, thinking about God's promise, thinking that when God fulfilled it his descendants would be as many as the stars in the sky. Each star seemed to stand for one of his descendants, and each grain of sand seemed to stand for one of his offspring. His thinking had substance and evidence. He kept nurturing his faith through thinking, until at one hundred years old his faith was fulfilled and he truly bore Isaac, the son of promise.

So God accomplished his promise through Abraham's faith. This is the principle by which Abraham, our father of faith, was trained by God. I believe the same principle is how God can train us too: we should think through hearing and think through seeing, nurture faith through thinking, and accomplish God's promise through faith. Amen.
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for teaching us through the story of the centurion what true faith is. Help us, like him, to trust Jesus with a humble heart, and to believe that every word of his has the power to change lives. May we depend on your word in our lives and bear witness to your great power. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: Soon afterwards, he went to a city called Nain. Many of his disciples, along with a great multitude, went with him.
Now when he came near to the gate of the city, behold, one who was dead was carried out, the only son of his mother, and she was a widow. Many people of the city were with her.
When the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her, and said to her, “Don’t cry.”
He came near and touched the coffin, and the bearers stood still. He said, “Young man, I tell you, arise!”
He who was dead sat up, and began to speak. And he gave him to his mother.
Fear took hold of all, and they glorified God, saying, “A great prophet has arisen among us!” and, “God has visited his people!”
This report went out concerning him in the whole of Judea, and in all the surrounding region.
b: This passage records Jesus performing a resurrection miracle in the town of Nain, raising from the dead the only son of a widow. It is a true expression of Jesus' compassionate heart: he saw the widow's grief and took the initiative to help her, even before she asked. Jesus' action shows his deep concern for human suffering.

The moment Jesus commanded the young man to rise shows his absolute authority over life and death. He did not come merely to comfort this grieving mother; he stepped in directly, changed her situation, and restored her family. The miracle amazed those around, who realized that God was at work among them through Jesus, and so they gave glory to God.

This passage reminds us that Jesus is not only a teacher but also our Savior, who can rescue us from the deepest despair. However dark our situation, Jesus can bring hope and life. His compassion and power are everywhere, and he is willing to step into our lives and bring change.
q: When you face hard situations in life, do you believe Jesus can bring change? How can you rely on his strength and compassion in difficulty?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for giving us Jesus, who is not only our Savior but also our help in hard times. Help us, in pain and despair, to rely on Jesus' compassion and great power, knowing that he can change everything. May our faith be strengthened in your love and bear witness to your great power. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: The disciples of John told him about all these things.
John, calling to himself two of his disciples, sent them to Jesus, saying, “Are you the one who is coming, or should we look for another?”
When the men had come to him, they said, “John the Baptizer has sent us to you, saying, ‘Are you he who comes, or should we look for another?’ ”
In that hour he cured many of diseases and plagues and evil spirits; and to many who were blind he gave sight.

Jesus answered them, “Go and tell John the things which you have seen and heard: that the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, and the poor have good news preached to them.
Blessed is he who finds no occasion for stumbling in me.”
b: This passage describes John the Baptist in prison, falling into confusion in the trial of his faith, and sending his disciples to ask Jesus whether he is the Messiah who was to come. It is a very human moment: even a great believer like John the Baptist can fall into doubt and confusion in adversity.

Jesus did not answer the question directly, but listed the miracles he had done to prove that he was the promised Messiah. He healed the sick, gave sight to the blind, raised the dead, and preached the good news to the poor, and these actions show the work and mission of the Messiah. Jesus' reply was meant to encourage John to hold on to his faith, recognizing that God's kingdom had already come through his deeds.

Jesus' last words, "Blessed is he who is not offended by me," remind us that when we face difficulty or confusion we should hold firm to our faith and not lose confidence in Christ because of challenging circumstances. We are called to accept in faith all that Jesus does, even when we do not fully understand.
q: When you face challenges to your faith, how do you keep your confidence in Jesus? When confusion and questions come, are you willing to return to Jesus' teaching and deeds to seek answers?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for showing us your truth and love through Jesus. When we face doubt and difficulty, strengthen our faith so that we do not stumble because of circumstances, and can keep believing that Jesus is the promised Savior. May we find peace and strength in your love. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: When John’s messengers had departed, he began to tell the multitudes about John, “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind?
But what did you go out to see? A man clothed in soft clothing? Behold, those who are gorgeously dressed, and live delicately, are in kings’ courts.
But what did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and much more than a prophet.
This is he of whom it is written, ‘Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way before you.’
“For I tell you, among those who are born of women there is not a greater prophet than John the Baptizer, yet he who is least in God’s Kingdom is greater than he.”
When all the people and the tax collectors heard this, they declared God to be just, having been baptized with John’s baptism.
But the Pharisees and the lawyers rejected the counsel of God, not being baptized by him themselves.
b: In this passage Jesus praises the greatness of John the Baptist and compares him with the other prophets. John was not a weak man, nor one who sought a life of luxury; he was God's messenger, appointed to prepare the way for the Messiah. Jesus points out that John was greater than all the prophets because he directly prepared for the Messiah's coming.

Yet Jesus also says that in God's kingdom the least is greater than John. This is not to belittle John, but to stress the uniqueness and surpassing nature of God's kingdom. When we enter God's kingdom, our identity and worth go beyond everything on earth; whatever our position in the world, in God's kingdom we are honored and valued.

The passage also says that all the people and the tax collectors, having been baptized with John's baptism, were willing to declare God just, while the Pharisees and the lawyers, by refusing John's baptism, rejected God's purpose for themselves. This reminds us that accepting God's call and obeying his will is the key to entering God's kingdom.
q: In your life, are you willing to obey God's will and accept his call? How can you make sure you find your true identity and worth in God's kingdom?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for preparing the way for us to receive Jesus through John the Baptist. Help us to be humble and obedient in life, to accept your call, and to enter your kingdom. May we find our true identity and worth in your kingdom and walk in your will in faith. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: “To what then should I compare the people of this generation? What are they like?
They are like children who sit in the marketplace, and call to one another, saying, ‘We piped to you, and you didn’t dance. We mourned, and you didn’t weep.’
For John the Baptizer came neither eating bread nor drinking wine, and you say, ‘He has a demon.’
The Son of Man has come eating and drinking, and you say, ‘Behold, a gluttonous man, and a drunkard; a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’
Wisdom is justified by all her children.”
b: This passage records Jesus' criticism of that generation. He says the people of this generation are like unreasonable, fussy children who refuse to respond rightly whatever the situation. They criticized John the Baptist as too severe, saying he had a demon, and then criticized Jesus for mixing with sinners, calling him a glutton and a drunkard. Neither John's fasting life nor Jesus' acceptance and compassion could satisfy these people.

Jesus points out that the people of this generation rejected God's messengers, and whether they were stern or loving, they were misunderstood and pushed away. This refusal and stubbornness show a closed heart: they refused God's grace because it did not match their expectations and standards.

Yet Jesus also reminds us that truly wise people recognize God's wisdom and works. Wisdom is justified by all her children; they are not blinded by worldly prejudice, but see the truth and love that God shows through different messengers and in different ways. We are called to be such children of wisdom, going beyond worldly eyes and accepting all that God gives.
q: When you face pressure from society and your surroundings, can you go beyond worldly prejudice and accept God's work and grace? How can you stay wise and hold to the truth in your life?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for showing us, through Jesus and John the Baptist, different spiritual paths. Give us wisdom so that we are not blinded by worldly prejudice, but can see your works and receive your grace. May we hold to the truth in our lives, become children of wisdom, and bear witness to your glory. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: One of the Pharisees invited him to eat with him. He entered into the Pharisee’s house, and sat at the table.
Behold, a woman in the city who was a sinner, when she knew that he was reclining in the Pharisee’s house, brought an alabaster jar of ointment.
Standing behind at his feet weeping, she began to wet his feet with her tears, and she wiped them with the hair of her head, kissed his feet, and anointed them with the ointment.
Now when the Pharisee who had invited him saw it, he said to himself, “This man, if he were a prophet, would have perceived who and what kind of woman this is who touches him, that she is a sinner.”
Jesus answered him, “Simon, I have something to tell you.” He said, “Teacher, say on.”
“A certain lender had two debtors. The one owed five hundred denarii, and the other fifty.
When they couldn’t pay, he forgave them both. Which of them therefore will love him most?”
Simon answered, “He, I suppose, to whom he forgave the most.” He said to him, “You have judged correctly.”

Turning to the woman, he said to Simon, “Do you see this woman? I entered into your house, and you gave me no water for my feet, but she has wet my feet with her tears, and wiped them with the hair of her head.
You gave me no kiss, but she, since the time I came in, has not ceased to kiss my feet.
You didn’t anoint my head with oil, but she has anointed my feet with ointment.
Therefore I tell you, her sins, which are many, are forgiven, for she loved much. But one to whom little is forgiven, loves little.”
He said to her, “Your sins are forgiven.”
Those who sat at the table with him began to say to themselves, “Who is this who even forgives sins?”
He said to the woman, “Your faith has saved you. Go in peace.”
b: This passage records an event in the house of Simon the Pharisee, where a sinful woman washed Jesus' feet with ointment and tears. It is a scene full of emotion and the meaning of redemption, and Jesus used the occasion to teach a deep truth about love and forgiveness.

The woman's action shows her deep love and reverence for Jesus. She washed his feet with tears and ointment, expressing her repentance and gratitude. Simon, a Pharisee, though he invited Jesus into his house, failed to truly understand Jesus' identity and mission. Through a parable Jesus points out that the one who is forgiven more loves more: this woman knew her sin was great, yet was forgiven by Jesus' grace, and so her love for Jesus was even deeper.

This passage reminds us that Jesus came into the world precisely to seek and save the lost. He does not care about our past sins but about whether we are willing to repent and love him. When we deeply experience Jesus' forgiving grace, our love and gratitude keep growing, and that love becomes the strength and motivation of our lives.
q: Because you know Jesus' forgiving grace deeply, do you love him more? How can you turn this love into concrete action in your life to honor him?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for giving us Jesus, whose love and forgiveness are our greatest treasure. Help us to experience this grace deeply and to respond to Jesus' love with all our hearts. May our lives be renewed by your forgiveness and become vessels that bear witness to your grace. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.
